label: Riemannian Curvature
notes: Welcome the class to Arnold's final appendix, where geometry returns dividends to mechanics. Stress the through-line: curvature is not an abstract tensor but the quantity that decides whether nearby motions stay together or fly apart. Promise the payoff, an honest geometric reason that long-range weather is unpredictable.

label: Parallel Transport
notes: Explain that on a curved surface there is no canonical way to compare vectors at different points; the connection supplies one by prescribing parallel transport. Emphasise the failure of path independence: dragging a vector around a loop rotates it, and that rotation angle is the first fingerprint of curvature we can actually see.

label: Covariant Derivative
notes: Introduce the covariant derivative as the rate of change of a field corrected so that genuinely parallel fields read as constant. Note that a geodesic is the curve whose velocity is parallel to itself, the straightest possible path. This sets up the comparison of neighbouring straight paths on the next slides.

label: Sectional Curvature
notes: Define sectional curvature as the Gaussian curvature of the surface swept by geodesics tangent to a chosen plane. Underline its operational meaning: it measures, to leading order, how the lengths of nearby parallel geodesics deviate. Positive means they bend toward each other, negative means they peel apart.

label: The Jacobi Equation
notes: Present the Jacobi equation as the linearisation of the geodesic flow about one geodesic. The separation field obeys a second-order equation in which curvature plays the role of a spring constant. Positive curvature gives an oscillator that refocuses deviations; negative curvature gives an inverted oscillator with runaway solutions.

label: Focusing vs Divergence
notes: Contrast the two model surfaces side by side. On the sphere, meridians launched parallel at the equator are forced to meet at the pole, the signature of focusing. On the saddle, two nearby geodesics separate without bound. Have students predict the sign of curvature from the picture before you confirm it.

label: Exponential Divergence
notes: Solve the Jacobi equation with constant negative curvature to expose hyperbolic growth. The separation swells like an exponential whose rate is the square root of the curvature magnitude. This is the geometric birth of sensitive dependence on initial conditions, the Lyapunov exponent written in the language of geometry.

label: Geometry of Lie Groups
notes: Shift to Arnold's reformulation of mechanics as geodesic flow on a Lie group carrying a one-sided invariant metric. The kinetic energy becomes the metric; the equations of motion become geodesic equations. Curvature is then computed algebraically from the commutator, turning a dynamical question into Lie-algebra bookkeeping.

label: Curvature from the Bracket
notes: Give the working formula: the right-invariant curvature is assembled from brackets and the inner product on the algebra. Reassure students that the messy terms reduce dramatically for the special directions we care about. The key output is a sign, and for the fluid group that sign will be negative in most sections.

label: The Ideal Fluid
notes: Introduce the punchline configuration space: volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of the flow domain. A fluid motion is a path in this infinite-dimensional group, and Euler's equations are exactly its geodesics for the kinetic-energy metric. Arnold's insight reframes hydrodynamics as Riemannian geometry on this group.

label: Negative Curvature & Weather
notes: Connect the threads: Arnold found that this diffeomorphism group has negative curvature in most two-dimensional sections. By the Jacobi mechanism, fluid trajectories diverge exponentially, so a tiny error in the initial state is amplified relentlessly. Cite his estimate that weeks-ahead forecasting is geometrically hopeless.

label: Summary
notes: Recap the logical chain in one breath: connection gives parallel transport, curvature measures its loop-defect, the Jacobi equation turns that into geodesic focusing or divergence, and on the fluid group divergence wins. Leave students with curvature as the bridge from pure geometry to the limits of prediction.
